what-is-diffraction-in-photography.question: What is diffraction in photography?
what-is-diffraction-in-photography.answer: Diffraction is the bending of light waves as they squeeze through a small aperture. The smaller the aperture (higher f-number), the more each point of light spreads into a fuzzy disk (the Airy disk) on the sensor. Once that disk grows larger than a pixel, fine detail blurs no matter how good the lens is.

what-aperture-is-sharpest.question: What aperture is sharpest?
what-aperture-is-sharpest.answer: Most lenses peak two or three stops down from wide open — typically f/4 to f/8 on full frame. That sweet spot balances lens aberrations (worst wide open) against diffraction (worse as you stop down). High-resolution sensors reach their diffraction limit earlier, so their usable sweet spot is narrower.

does-diffraction-depend-on-sensor.question: Does diffraction depend on the sensor?
does-diffraction-depend-on-sensor.answer: The optical effect depends only on aperture and the wavelength of light — but how visible it is depends on pixel size. A 61 MP full-frame sensor has ~3.8 µm pixels and shows diffraction softening around f/5.6, while a 12 MP sensor with big pixels stays crisp to f/11. Smaller sensors hit the limit at wider apertures for the same megapixel count.
